title: He wasn’t the one foaming at the mouth.
paragraphs: He wasn’t the one foaming at the mouth.
He wasn’t the one convulsing in the dirt.
But he was breaking too.
The character I almost overlooked in Mark 9 was not the demon-possessed boy.
It was his father.

A man exhausted by disappointment.
A man carrying his son’s torment in his own chest.
A man who had probably prayed until prayer started sounding tired.
A man who brought his boy to the disciples and still walked straight into another heartbreak.
And then it spills out.

“If You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.”
Not just help him.
Help us.
That line is heavy.

Because this father was not watching suffering from a distance. He was living inside it. Every seizure stole from the boy’s body, but it also tore at the father’s soul. Every failed attempt. Every public scene. Every whisper from the crowd. Every night without answers. He was drowning too.
And when Jesus answered, He went straight for the wound:
“‘If You can’! All things are possible for one who believes.” (Mark 9:23)
Then comes one of the most honest cries in the whole Bible:
“I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24)

That is not polished faith.
That is not stage faith.
That is bruised faith. Limping faith. Barely-breathing faith.
And Jesus did not reject it.
That part wrecks me.

Because many of us think we need to come to Christ with clean certainty, strong theology, and unshaken confidence. But this father came with faith mixed with fear. Hope tangled up with pain. Trust interrupted by trauma.
And Jesus still moved.
Here’s what we miss:

The miracle was not just for the boy.
Grace was reaching for the father too.

Jesus was not merely confronting a demon.
He was rescuing a household.
He was answering the cry of a parent who had run out of strength but had not stopped running to Jesus.
That is the Gospel.

We do not come to Jesus because our faith is flawless.
We come because He is merciful.
We are not saved by the strength of our grip on Him, but by the strength of His grip on us. Christ receives weak people, trembling people, desperate people. At the cross, He made full payment for sin. In His resurrection, He secured real hope for ruined hearts. The father brought his broken son. Jesus gave what no human power could give.
And maybe that is you.

You are not demon-possessed.
But your house is heavy.
Your prayers feel delayed.
Your faith has cracks in it.
You still believe.
But barely.
Then borrow this father’s prayer.
“Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.”
That prayer still reaches heaven.
And Jesus still answers broken people who fall at His feet.

Don’t hide your weakness from Christ.
Bring it.
Bring the fear.
Bring the tears.
Bring the half-shaking faith.

He is still mighty enough to heal what hell has touched.
He is still tender enough to carry the one everyone else overlooked.
